COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY #1

  • Dr. Mihai Socaciu
  • mihai.socaciu@umfcluj.ro

General Principles #2

  • • different tissues of the body have different
  • rates of linear X-ray attenuation
  • → differences in the X-ray transmission
  • intensity (a difference in the “density” of
  • film penetration)

General Principles #3

  • Computerised Tomography:
  • - uses the X-ray beam in a non-conventional manner,
  • generating a cross sectional image of the patient
  • - the “slice” represents a bi-dimensional
  • image → computed reconstruction
  • of multiple angular projections
  • of the selected section
  • - the X-ray beam penetrates only the section of interest,
  • without passing through neighboring anatomy

Page 4 #4

Computerized Tomography: #5

  • Components of CT equipment :
  • Scanner
  • Workstation
  • Display

The X-ray beam collimation: #6

  • - generates the thickness of the slice
  • - both before and after X-rays penetrates the
  • body
  • - reduces scattering of
  • radiation
  • - improves the spatial and
  • densimetric resolution

conventional CT #7

  • → Spiral CT
  • → multi-spiral/multi-detector CT
  • (High-speed)
  • Purpose :
  • “optimal diagnostic imaging using o low (minimal)
  • dose of iradiation”

CT Image #8

  • ! The CT number of every single pixel
  • represents the average value of x-ray beam
  • attenuation of all anatomical structures in the
  • representative voxel

• HypoDENSE #9

  • CT Image – density!
  • • IsoDENSE
  • • HyperDENSE
  • • positive values
  • The human eye can perceive
  • simultaneously a limited number of H.U.
  • grey-scale numbers
  • • negative values

Windows manipulation #10

  • Window Level

Dynamic scanning #11

  • Arterial Phase
  • Native scan
  • (Portho)-Venous phase

Why contrast? #12

  • • Limited “contrast resolution” = Dynamic range of native CT
  •  Can hardly differentiate between tissues
  • • Need for a dynamic assessment of vascularity
  • • For abdominal CTs, i.v. contrast in MANDATORY, except:
  • • Pneumoperitoneum (perforation)
  • • Positive Dg of occlusion
  • • Assessment of stones (esp. kidney)
  • • Catheter placement, metal foreign objects etc.

What contrast? #13

  • • Iodine based – preferably non-ionic, iso/hypoosmolar
  • (i.e. Iopamiro, Omnipaque, Optiray, Ultravist)
  • CONTRAINDICTIONS:
  • • Known allergy
  • • Impaired renal function
  • ➢ Creatinin > 1,5 mg%
  • ➢ Creatinin clearance: < 30 ml/min/1,73 sqm – NO
  • 30-50 ml/min/1,73 sqm – i.v. fluids
  • 51-80 ml/min/1,73 sqm – oral fluids
  • • Relative: Poliallergic patiens; Hyperthyroidism; Recent
  • treatment with Metformin (oral antidiabetic drug)

Clinical Considerations #14

  • Advantages
  • • good 3D visualization
  • • high spatial resolution
  • • better density (contrast) resolution then conventional Xray
  • Best usage:
  • • emergency
  • • lungs
  • • bone (cortical) / calcifications
  • • best all-round radiology method

Clinical Considerations #15

  • Disadvantages
  • • the price of the investigation / accessibility (?)
  • • high dose of radiation
  • • contrast agents with allergenic potential /
  • secondary effects

Role of CT in hepato-billiary evaluation #16

  • • Chronic hepatopathy - limited role !
  • • Hepatic Cirrhosis
  • • dimensions (> Left lobe, caudate lobe; < Right lobe)
  • • contour
  • • changes in the portal circulation
  • • the presence of ascitis
  • • +/- nodular pattern

Page 17 #17

Tumors #18

  • Hepatocarcinoma (HCC)
  • • the nodular type
  • • the difuse type
  • • Portal vein invasion!
  • • arterial phase: hyperenhancement – arterial supply (wash-in)
  • • portal phase: isoenhancement
  • • late phase: hypoenhancement – wash-out

• the nodular type #19

• the difuse type + PV invasion #20

Benign Tu : Hepatic Hemangioma #21

  • • Asymptomatic
  • • Usually discovered incidentally on ultrasound / CT
  • • Hypodense in the native phase
  • • Arterial Phase – hyperenhancing peripheral globular
  • • Porthal Phase – continuous centripetal enhancement
  • • Parenchimal Phase – continuous centripetal enhancement

Benign Tu : Hepatic Hemangioma #22

Hepatic Metastasis #23

  • • Hystory of cancer
  • • multiple nodules, similar dimensions and aspect
  • • Rim enhancement (most) – arterial phase
  • • Complete wash-out = hypodense in portal phase
  • • ! Small lesions could be hard to distinguish from
  • cysts

Hepatic Metastasis #24

Liver abscess #25

  • • May mimic a metastasis
  • • No enhancement in the center (necrosis)
  • • Thick enhancing band +/- enhancing wall

CT Imaging of the gallbladder #26

  • • Stones are not always visible (may be isodense to
  • the bile) => Ultrasound assessment is better
  • • Best suited in complicated cholecystitis
  • • GB tumors – usually invade the liver, look like mets

Cholecystitis #27

GB tumor #28

Extra-hepatic Cholestasis #29

  • • Mechanical
  • Obstruction of the
  • billiary tree
  • • Dilatation of the
  • intra-hepatic billiary
  • branches
  • •The “duble-duct” sign

CT Imaging of the pancreas – #30

  • acute pancreatitis
  • • Edematous / necrotic
  • • Increasing in volume of the pancreatic space
  • • Inflammatory changes of the peri-pancreatic fat
  • • Necrosis
  • • Fluid collections, pseudocysts
  • • Bleeding, pseudoaneurisms
  • • CT Score

Acute pancreatitis - necrotic #31

Chronic Pancreatitis #32

  • • Parenchimal / ductal calcifications
  • • Wirsung duct dilation
  • • Atrophy
  • • Pseudocysts / walled-off necrotic collections

Chronic Pancreatitis #33

Pancreatic Tumor #34

  • • Solid Nodule
  • (rarely cystic-like formation)
  • • Poor Delineation
  • • Adenocc - hypoenhancing
  • • Invasion of the adjacent
  • organs/vessels

Pancreatic Tumors #35

  • → sugestive for
  • Dilatation of WD and CBD: “double duct” sign
  • a cephalic pancreatic or ampulary cc.

Pancreatic Tumors #36

  • Cystic tumors:
  • differential diagnosis with chronic pancreatitis (pseudocysts)

Pancreatic Tumors #37

  • Evaluation of surgical resectability – role of CT

CT Imaging of the bowel and colon #38

  • • EnteroCT – water distention of the bowels through use of
  • purgatives:
  • ➢ No solid food the day before
  • ➢ 2 l of Macrogol (Fortrans) the evening before
  • ➢ 1,5 l of Fortrans before the examination
  • ➢ 0,5 l of water just before the examination
  • • ColonoCT – water distention of the colon through enema:
  • ➢ No solid food the day before
  • ➢ 4 l of Macrogol (Fortrans) the evening before
  • ➢ Water enema on the CT table
  • ➢ Hyperdense contrast can be used, especialy when
  • suspecting a fistula
  • • CT pneumocolon – air distention of the colon through inflation
  • ➢ Needs similar preparation the day before
  • ➢ Used for virtual colonoscopy

CT Imaging of the bowel and colon #39

  • • Best imaging method for the bowels (along with MRI)
  • • Is complementary to endoscopy
  • ➢ Doesn’t show surface changes of the mucosa
  • ➢ Can show involvement of the layers of the bowel
  • ➢ Water distention – allows depiction of protrusive
  • tumors and presence of stenosis
  • •Main applications:
  • ➢ Inflammatory – ac. Apendicitis + peritonitis, IBD..
  • ➢ Digestive perforation, fistulas
  • ➢ Tumors, occlusion, volvulus, intussusception
  • ➢ Acute bleeding

Acute appendicitis #40

  • • Increase in thickness (>6 mm)
  • •Contrast uptake
  • •Inflammatory changes (edema) around the appendix
  • •Perforation => peritoneal fluid, abscesses

CT pneumocolon #41

  • Polyps: tiny nodular enhancing
  • images, multiple, - -
  • Lesions > 1 cm have a high
  • susceptibility to malignancy - -
  • (htp confirmed carcinoma)
  • CT Pneumocolon in a patient with
  • change in bowel habit and weight
  • loss, The only abnormality on CT
  • pneumocolon was a lipoma
  • of the ileo-caecal valve - -.
  • The CT attenuation value is
  • pathognomonic.

CT pneumo-colon – virtual colonoscopy #42

CT Imaging of the spleen #43

  • • Characteristic: inhomogeneous enhancement in
  • the arterial phase
  • • Best use – trauma -> dilaceration, hematomas
  • • Increased in size in:
  • • Cirrhosis, acute hepatitis
  • • Infectious diseases
  • • Haematologic disorders
  • • Deposition diseases (ex: Gaucher)
  • • Solid tumors might be hard to differentiate
